title: Stapleton and Vasquez: none stand without mercy
source_text: XXX. Quippe nullus eorum est, quantum equidem novi, qui dicere audeat fideles propria & sibi inhaerente justitia fretos, posse coram severo tribunali Dei consistere, & in eo reos non peragi, etiamsi Deus illos absque misericordia judicet: Aut qui reclamet Stapletono fatenti, Si secundum severum judicium Deus homines judicaret, nullam hominis justitiam in isto judicio stare posse: Lib. de Justif. cap. 14. Et Vasquezio agnoscenti unumquemque nostrum, tam ante justificationem, quam post justificationem, teneri cum Psalmista dicere, Ne intres in judicium cum servo tuo; Quoniam, nisi Deus nos misericordia sua praeveniat, ut a peccatis justificemur, non poterimus non in judicio Dei damnari. Et adhuc post justificationem a peccato mortali, multa venialia manent, quae, nisi Dei misericordia deleantur, priusquam ad judicium Dei vocemur, non poterit homo omnino justificari, hoc est, omnino effugere Dei judicium & ultionem. Tom. 2. in 1. 2. Disp. 222. Cap. 6. num. 44.
pass_a_gloss: For there is none of them, so far as I know, who dares say that the faithful, relying on their own inherent righteousness, can stand before God’s severe tribunal and not be prosecuted as guilty there even if God judges them without mercy; or who would cry out against Stapleton confessing that if God judged men according to severe judgment, no human righteousness could stand in that judgment (On Justification, ch. 14); and against Vasquez acknowledging that each of us, both before and after justification, is bound to say with the Psalmist, Enter not into judgment with your servant—because unless God prevents us with his mercy so that we are justified from sins, we cannot but be damned in God’s judgment. And even after justification from mortal sin many venials remain which, unless deleted by God’s mercy before we are called to God’s judgment, a man cannot be altogether justified—that is, altogether escape God’s judgment and vengeance (Tom. 2 on 1a2ae, Disp. 222, ch. 6, n. 44).
pass_b_english: No Roman doctor dares claim inherent justice stands God’s severe bar without mercy.
Stapleton and Vasquez: say with the Psalmist—enter not into judgment; venials still need mercy.
